title: Introduction to Conic Sections
summary: This lesson introduces the four basic conic sections—circle, parabola, ellipse, and hyperbola—and explains how they arise from slicing a cone. Students learn the key features and standard equations that describe each shape.
objectives: Identify the four types of conic sections and their visual characteristics
State the standard form of the equation for each conic
Explain how the eccentricity distinguishes the conics
Describe real‑world objects that correspond to each conic
Compare the shapes based on their definitions
prerequisites: Students should be comfortable with basic algebra, plotting points on a coordinate plane, and the concept of distance between two points.
why: Conic sections appear in many engineering and scientific contexts, such as satellite orbits (ellipses) and satellite dish designs (parabolas). Understanding their properties helps predict motion and design efficient structures.
In everyday life, the shapes of wheels, arches, and lenses are conic sections. Recognising these forms lets students see mathematics in the world around them.

sections.heading: What Is a Conic Section?
sections.body:
Imagine a solid ice‑cream cone that has two identical parts, one pointing up and one pointing down, glued together at their tips. Mathematicians call this shape a **double‑napped cone**.  
> **Definition:** A *conic section* is the curve you obtain when a flat surface (a plane) cuts through this double‑napped cone.

The word *section* simply means “the part that is left after cutting”. So a conic section is the *section* of the cone that remains visible on the cutting plane.

Why does this idea matter?  Many familiar curves—circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas—can all be produced in this single, geometric way.  By changing only the angle at which we slice the cone, we get a completely different curve.  This unifies several seemingly unrelated shapes under one simple principle, which is useful in physics, engineering, and astronomy.

### How the angle of the plane changes the curve

Think of the cone standing upright, with its tip at the origin.  The cone’s surface makes a fixed angle, say $\theta$, with the vertical axis.  Now imagine a flat board (the plane) intersecting the cone.  The crucial factor is the **inclination** of the board, i.e., the angle $\phi$ between the plane and the same vertical axis.

- If the plane is **parallel to the base** of the cone (so $\phi = 90^\circ$), the intersection is a perfect **circle**.  
- If the plane is **tilted a little**, but still **steeper than the cone’s side** ($\phi < \theta$), the cut produces an **ellipse**—a stretched circle.  
- If the plane is **tilted exactly as steep as the cone’s side** ($\phi = \theta$), the intersection becomes a **parabola**, the curve that describes the path of a thrown ball.  
- If the plane is **tilted even more gently**, so it cuts both nappes of the cone ($\phi > \theta$), the result is a **hyperbola**, which looks like two open arms.

These four cases cover all possible non‑degenerate conic sections.  (A *degenerate* case would be a single point or a pair of intersecting lines, which happen when the plane passes through the tip of the cone.)

### Visualising with everyday objects

Picture a sliced orange.  If you cut it straight across the middle, the exposed surface is a circle.  If you slice it at a slight angle, the exposed surface becomes an ellipse—notice how the shape looks longer in one direction.  Now imagine a very shallow cut that just grazes the surface of the orange; the exposed curve looks like a parabola, opening outward.  Finally, think of a knife that passes through the orange and continues on the other side, creating two separate curves that open away from each other—this is analogous to a hyperbola.

> **In daily life:** The shape of satellite dishes (parabolas) and the orbits of planets (ellipses) are both conic sections that arise from this simple cutting idea.

### Connecting the geometry to algebra

When we write the equation of a conic section in a coordinate system, the different angles of the cutting plane translate into different algebraic forms.  For example, a circle centred at the origin has the equation  

$$x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2},$$  

where $r$ is the radius.  An ellipse with semi‑axes $a$ and $b$ is described by  

$$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1,$$  

and a parabola opening upward can be written as  

$$y = \frac{1}{4p}x^{2},$$  

where $p$ is the distance from the vertex to the focus.  The hyperbola’s equation  

$$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$$  

reflects the fact that the plane cuts both nappes of the cone.

> **Remember:** All these algebraic formulas come from the same geometric process—changing the tilt of a plane that slices a double‑napped cone.

Understanding conic sections as slices of a cone gives a powerful visual intuition.  It shows that a wide variety of curves share a common origin, making it easier to recognise their properties and to apply them in real‑world problems.

sections.heading: The Circle
sections.body:
A circle is one of the simplest and most familiar shapes in geometry.  
Imagine you have a nail hammered into a piece of wood and you tie a string to it. If you keep the string tight and move a pencil around while keeping the string stretched, the pencil tip will draw a perfect round line. Every point on that line is **exactly the same distance** from the nail.  

> **Definition:** A *circle* is the set of all points in a plane that are at a fixed distance, called the *radius*, from a single fixed point, called the *centre*.

The centre is the nail, the radius is the length of the string, and the drawn line is the circle itself. This idea is useful because it gives us a clear way to describe a round shape with just two pieces of information: where the centre is and how far out the circle reaches.

### Coordinates and the centre

When we work with algebra, we place the picture on a coordinate grid. The centre of the circle gets coordinates $(h,k)$, where $h$ tells us how far left or right the centre is from the origin, and $k$ tells us how far up or down it is. The radius, a single positive number, is written $r$.

### Deriving the equation

Take any point $(x,y)$ that lies on the circle. By the definition of a circle, the distance from $(x,y)$ to the centre $(h,k)$ must equal $r$. The distance between two points in the plane is given by the *distance formula*, which comes from the Pythagorean theorem:

$$\text{distance} = \sqrt{(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2}.$$

Setting this distance equal to $r$ gives

$$\sqrt{(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2} = r.$$

To remove the square root, we square both sides (remembering that $r$ is non‑negative, so squaring does not change the equality):

$$ (x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2. $$

This compact formula tells us exactly which points belong to the circle. If you plug in the coordinates of a point and the formula holds true, the point is on the circle; if not, the point lies either inside or outside.

> **Note:** The symbols $h$ and $k$ are just letters; they could be any numbers. They are called the *coordinates of the centre*.

### Special case: centre at the origin

If the centre happens to be at the origin $(0,0)$, the formula simplifies because $h=0$ and $k=0$:

$$ x^2 + y^2 = r^2. $$

This is the version you often see first in textbooks because it is the cleanest. It says that every point whose $x$‑coordinate and $y$‑coordinate satisfy this equation lies exactly $r$ units from the origin.

### Using the equation

The equation is powerful because it lets us do many things without drawing:

* **Find the radius** if we know the centre and a point on the circle: plug the point into the equation and solve for $r$.
* **Check whether a point is inside** the circle: compute $(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2$ and compare it to $r^2$. If the result is smaller, the point is inside; if larger, it is outside.
* **Translate the circle**: moving the centre from $(0,0)$ to $(h,k)$ just adds $h$ and $k$ inside the squares, as shown in the general formula.

> **In daily life:** Wheels, coins, and round tables are all circles. Knowing the centre and radius lets engineers design gears that fit together perfectly.

### Common pitfalls

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to square the radius when writing the equation. The correct form is $(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2$, not $(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r$. Leaving out the square changes the shape completely.

### Quick recap

* A circle = all points at the same distance $r$ from a centre $(h,k)$.
* Distance formula → equation $(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2$.
* If the centre is the origin, the equation becomes $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$.
* The equation helps us calculate radius, test points, and move circles around the plane.

> **Remember:** The circle’s equation is just a tidy way of writing “stay exactly $r$ units away from $(h,k)$.” Once you see the pattern, you can recognize circles hidden inside more complicated algebraic expressions.

sections.heading: The Parabola
sections.body:
A parabola is the set of all points that are **exactly the same distance** from two fixed objects: a single point called the *focus* and a straight line called the *directrix*.  
Think of the focus as a tiny lamp that shines light, and the directrix as a flat wall. Any point on the curve is positioned so that the distance to the lamp equals the distance to the wall. This simple rule creates a smooth, U‑shaped curve that opens either upward, downward, leftward, or rightward.

> **Definition:** A parabola is the locus of points $P$ such that $d(P,\text{focus}) = d(P,\text{directrix})$.

Why does this definition matter? Because it gives us a way to describe many natural and engineered shapes with a single equation. For example, the path of a ball thrown in the air (ignoring air resistance) follows a parabola, and the reflective surface of a satellite dish is shaped like one so that signals from the focus are sent out as parallel beams.

### Building the equation

1. **Place the focus and directrix**  
   Choose a convenient coordinate system. Suppose the focus is at $(h, k + p)$ and the directrix is the horizontal line $y = k - p$, where $p>0$ measures the distance from the vertex (the point halfway between focus and directrix) to each of them.

2. **Write the distance condition**  
   For a generic point $P=(x,y)$ on the curve, the distance to the focus is  
   $$\sqrt{(x-h)^2 + (y-(k+p))^2}.$$  
   The distance to the directrix is the vertical distance  
   $$|y-(k-p)|.$$

3. **Set the distances equal and square**  
   $$\sqrt{(x-h)^2 + (y-(k+p))^2}=|y-(k-p)|.$$  
   Squaring both sides removes the square root and the absolute value (since both sides are non‑negative):  
   $$(x-h)^2 + (y-(k+p))^2 = (y-(k-p))^2.$$

4. **Simplify**  
   Expand the right‑hand side:  
   $$(y-(k-p))^2 = (y-k+p)^2 = (y-k)^2 + 2p(y-k) + p^2.$$  
   Expand the left‑hand side similarly and cancel the common $(y-k)^2$ terms. After cancellation we obtain  
   $$(x-h)^2 = 4p\,(y-k).$$  

5. **Introduce the constant $a$**  
   Let $a = \frac{1}{4p}$, or equivalently $4p = \frac{1}{a}$. Then the equation becomes the **standard vertical form**  
   $$y - k = a\,(x - h)^2.$$

If the parabola opens left or right instead of up or down, we start with a vertical directrix $x = h - p$ and a focus at $(h + p, k)$. Repeating the same steps gives the **standard horizontal form**  
$$x - h = a\,(y - k)^2.$$

> **Note:** The constant $a$ controls how “wide” or “narrow” the parabola is. Larger $|a|$ makes the curve steeper; smaller $|a|$ spreads it out.

### Using the formulas

- The point $(h,k)$ is the **vertex**, the turning point of the parabola.  
- The focus lies a distance $\frac{1}{4a}$ from the vertex along the axis of symmetry.  
- The directrix is a line the same distance on the opposite side of the vertex.

These relationships let us read geometric information directly from the equation, and conversely, to write an equation when we know the focus and directrix.

> **In daily life:** The shape of a flashlight’s reflector is a parabola. Light rays that start at the focus bounce off the surface and travel out as a parallel beam, which is why the beam stays tight over long distances.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting that the standard forms $y-k = a(x-h)^2$ and $x-h = a(y-k)^2$ apply only when the axis of symmetry is vertical or horizontal, respectively. If the parabola is tilted, a rotation of axes is required before using these simple formulas.

Remember that a parabola is defined by a simple distance rule, and that rule leads directly to the tidy algebraic forms above. Once you can identify the vertex $(h,k)$ and the constant $a$, you can sketch the curve, locate its focus and directrix, and apply the shape to real‑world problems.

sections.heading: The Ellipse
sections.body:
Imagine you have two pins pushed into a piece of cardboard. If you stretch a loop of string around the pins, then pull the loop tight with a pencil and draw the shape you get, you have just created an **ellipse**.  

> **Definition:** An ellipse is the set of all points $P$ in a plane such that the sum of the distances from $P$ to two fixed points (called the *foci*) is a constant value.

The two pins are the foci, usually labelled $F_1$ and $F_2$. For any point $P$ on the curve, the distances $PF_1$ and $PF_2$ add up to the same number, no matter where $P$ is placed on the ellipse. This constant sum is larger than the distance between the foci, otherwise the shape would collapse into a straight line.

Why does this definition matter? It tells us how to locate every point on the ellipse without having to draw it. It also explains why ellipses appear in nature: the path of a planet around the Sun follows this rule, with the Sun at one focus, because the gravitational force makes the total distance traveled in a given time follow the same rule.

### From the definition to an equation

To turn the wordy definition into a formula, place the ellipse so that its centre is at the point $(h,k)$ and the line joining the foci lies along the $x$‑axis. Let the distance from the centre to each focus be $c$, and let $a$ be half of the constant sum of distances (so the total sum is $2a$). The longest radius of the ellipse, measured from the centre to the farthest point on the curve, is called the *semi‑major axis* and has length $a$. The shortest radius, measured perpendicular to the major axis, is the *semi‑minor axis* with length $b$. These three lengths satisfy the relationship  

$$c^2 = a^2 - b^2.$$

Now pick any point $(x,y)$ on the ellipse. Its distances to the foci are  

$$PF_1 = \sqrt{(x-h-c)^2 + (y-k)^2},\qquad PF_2 = \sqrt{(x-h+c)^2 + (y-k)^2}.$$

Adding them and setting the sum equal to $2a$ gives  

$$\sqrt{(x-h-c)^2 + (y-k)^2} + \sqrt{(x-h+c)^2 + (y-k)^2} = 2a.$$

If we square both sides twice and simplify, the messy square‑roots disappear and we obtain the clean *standard equation* of an ellipse:

$$\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2} = 1.$$

> **Note:** The letters $a$ and $b$ are always the semi‑major and semi‑minor axes, even if the ellipse is turned sideways. The larger denominator belongs to the direction of the major axis.

### Understanding the symbols

- **Centre $(h,k)$** – the midpoint between the two foci; it is the point about which the ellipse is symmetric.
- **Semi‑major axis $a$** – half the longest diameter; it points along the line through the foci.
- **Semi‑minor axis $b$** – half the shortest diameter; it is perpendicular to the major axis.
- **Foci** – the two special points inside the ellipse; they are not on the edge but lie on the major axis at a distance $c$ from the centre.

If $a = b$, the denominators are equal and the equation becomes  

$$\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{a^2} = 1,$$

which simplifies to the equation of a **circle**. So a circle is just a special case of an ellipse where the two foci coincide at the centre.

> **In daily life:** The shape of a whispering gallery in a dome, the orbit of a satellite, and the cross‑section of a pipe that is cut at an angle are all ellipses. Engineers use the formula $\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}+\frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1$ to design these objects precisely.

### A quick check

Suppose an ellipse is centred at the origin $(0,0)$, has $a=5$ and $b=3$. Its equation is  

$$\frac{x^2}{25} + \frac{y^2}{9} = 1.$$

Pick the point $(3,0)$. Plugging in, $\frac{9}{25}+0=0.36$, which is less than $1$, so $(3,0)$ lies **inside** the ellipse. Try $(5,0)$: $\frac{25}{25}+0=1$, so this point is **on** the ellipse, confirming that $a$ really is the distance from the centre to the farthest point on the $x$‑axis.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting that $a$ is always the *larger* of the two axis lengths. If you swap $a$ and $b$, the equation still looks correct but it now describes an ellipse that is rotated 90°, which changes the location of the foci.

Remember, the ellipse is all about a constant sum of distances. The algebraic equation $\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}+\frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1$ is just a convenient way to capture that geometric idea on paper.

sections.heading: The Hyperbola
sections.body:
Imagine two fixed points on a flat surface; we call them the **foci** (singular: focus). A hyperbola is the collection of all points whose distances to these two foci differ by the same amount, no matter where you stand on the curve. In other words, if you pick any point $P$ on the hyperbola, measure its distance $d_1$ to the first focus and $d_2$ to the second focus, then the absolute value of $d_1-d_2$ is a constant number $2a$ (the same for every point on the curve).

> **Definition:** A hyperbola is the set of points $P$ such that $|\,\text{dist}(P,F_1)-\text{dist}(P,F_2)\,|=2a$, where $F_1$ and $F_2$ are the two foci and $a>0$ is a fixed length.

Why does this rule matter? It gives a simple geometric way to draw the curve using only a ruler and a string, just as the circle can be drawn by keeping a constant distance from a single point. The “difference of distances” condition also appears in physics: the path of a signal that reaches two antennas at the same time forms a hyperbola, because the travel‑time difference is proportional to the distance difference.

### From the definition to an equation

To turn the word picture into algebra, place the hyperbola’s centre at $(h,k)$ and align its axes with the coordinate axes. Let the foci lie on the horizontal line through the centre, at $(h-c,k)$ and $(h+c,k)$, where $c>0$ is the distance from the centre to each focus. For any point $(x,y)$ on the curve we have  

$$\bigl|\,\sqrt{(x-h-c)^2+(y-k)^2}\;-\;\sqrt{(x-h+c)^2+(y-k)^2}\,\bigr|=2a.$$

Squaring both sides, simplifying, and using the relationship $c^2=a^2+b^2$ (which emerges from the algebra) leads to the compact **standard equation** of a horizontally‑opening hyperbola:

$$\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}\;-\;\frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1.$$

Here $a$ controls how far the branches open from the centre, while $b$ determines how steeply they rise. The foci are at $(h\pm c,\,k)$ with $c=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, so the distance between the foci is $2c$.

If the hyperbola opens vertically instead of horizontally, the roles of $x$ and $y$ swap, giving  

$$\frac{(y-k)^2}{a^2}\;-\;\frac{(x-h)^2}{b^2}=1.$$

### Visualising the shape

Think of a pair of opposite‑shaped arms reaching out from the centre, never meeting. As you move farther from the centre, the branches become more like straight lines. Those asymptotic lines are given by the equations  

$$y-k=\pm\frac{b}{a}(x-h)$$  

for the horizontal case. They are not part of the hyperbola, but they guide its direction.

> **In daily life:** The set of points where a sound reaches two microphones with a fixed time difference forms a hyperbola. Engineers use this fact to locate the source of a noise by intersecting two such hyperbolas.

### Common pitfalls

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting the absolute value in the definition. Without it, the equation would only describe one branch of the hyperbola, because the distance difference could be positive or negative depending on which focus is farther.

### Remember the key pieces

> **Remember:**  
> • $a$ = half the constant difference of distances.  
> • $c$ = distance from centre to each focus, with $c^2=a^2+b^2$.  
> • The standard form $\displaystyle\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}-\frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1$ describes a hyperbola opening left‑right; swap $x$ and $y$ for up‑down.

Understanding the hyperbola as “constant difference of distances” links a simple geometric idea to a powerful algebraic tool, and it opens the door to many applications in astronomy, navigation, and engineering.

sections.heading: Eccentricity and Classification
sections.body:
Eccentricity is a single number that tells us how “stretched’’ a conic section is.  
We write it as the letter $e$.  By looking only at the value of $e$ we can tell whether the curve is a circle, an ellipse, a parabola, or a hyperbola.

> **Definition:** The *eccentricity* $e$ of a conic section is the ratio  

$$e=\frac{c}{a}$$  

where $c$ is the distance from the centre (or vertex) to a focus, and $a$ is the distance from the centre (or vertex) to a vertex along the main axis.  

The symbols $c$ and $a$ appear in the standard equations of each conic, so $e$ can be computed directly from those equations.

---

### Why a single number works

All conic sections are produced by slicing a cone with a plane.  
If the plane cuts the cone almost parallel to its side, the slice is very “flat’’ – that is a parabola.  
If the plane is more steep, the slice is rounder – an ellipse, and if the plane is exactly perpendicular to the cone’s axis, the slice is a perfect circle.  

The ratio $c/a$ measures exactly how far the focus is from the centre compared with the overall size of the curve.  
When the focus sits right at the centre ($c=0$) the curve is perfectly round, giving $e=0$.  
When the focus moves outward but stays inside the curve ($0<c<a$) the shape becomes an ellipse, so $0<e<1$.  
If the focus is exactly on the edge of the curve ($c=a$) the curve opens forever – a parabola, and $e=1$.  
When the focus lies outside the curve ($c>a$) the curve splits into two branches – a hyperbola, giving $e>1$.

Thus the single number $e$ captures the whole family of shapes.

> **Note:** The same definition works for all four conics; only the meaning of “centre’’ or “vertex’’ changes slightly.  For a parabola we take the vertex as the reference point, because a parabola has no centre.

---

### Everyday comparison

Imagine you are holding a rubber band stretched between two fingers.  
If the fingers are together, the band forms a perfect circle – the focus (the centre) is exactly at the middle, so $e=0$.  
If you pull the fingers apart a little, the band becomes an oval (ellipse); the focus moves away from the centre but stays inside, giving $0<e<1$.  
If you keep pulling until the band is just about to break and becomes a single, open curve, you have a parabola – the focus is now on the edge, $e=1$.  
Pull even further and the band snaps into two separate arcs that open away from each other – a hyperbola, with $e>1$.

> **In daily life:** Eccentricity is used in satellite orbits.  A satellite in a circular orbit has $e=0$; an elliptical orbit (most real satellites) has $0<e<1$; a comet on a parabolic escape trajectory has $e=1$; and a spacecraft on a hyperbolic fly‑by has $e>1$.

---

### Computing $e$ from the standard equations

For each conic we can read $a$ and $c$ directly:

* **Circle:** $x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}$ → $a=r$, $c=0$ → $e=0$.
* **Ellipse:** $\displaystyle \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ with $a>b$ → $c=\sqrt{a^{2}-b^{2}}$, so $e=\frac{\sqrt{a^{2}-b^{2}}}{a}$.
* **Parabola:** $y^{2}=4px$ → $a=p$, $c=p$ → $e=1$.
* **Hyperbola:** $\displaystyle \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ → $c=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$, so $e=\frac{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}{a}$.

> **Remember:** $e$ is always a non‑negative number.  Its value tells you the type of conic instantly.

---

### Common mistake

> **Common mistake:** Thinking that a larger $a$ always means a “bigger’’ conic.  The shape is determined by the *ratio* $c/a$, not by $a$ alone.  Two ellipses can have the same $a$ but different $b$, giving different eccentricities and therefore different shapes.

By keeping the single number $e$ in mind, you can quickly classify any conic section and understand how its geometry changes as the focus moves relative to the centre.

sections.heading: Real‑World Examples of Conics
sections.body:
Conic sections are not just abstract curves on a graph; they describe many shapes we see and use every day.  
Understanding where circles, parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas appear in the real world helps us remember their equations and why they matter.

A **circle** is the set of all points that are the same distance (the radius $r$) from a fixed point (the centre $(h,k)$).  
$$ (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2 $$  
> **In daily life:** The face of a clock, a round swimming pool, and the cross‑section of a pipe are all circles. When engineers design a wheel, they use the circle equation to ensure every point on the rim stays the same distance from the axle, giving smooth rotation.

A **parabola** is the curve where every point is equally distant from a fixed point (the focus) and a straight line (the directrix). Its standard form is  
$$ y = ax^2+bx+c $$  
or, with vertex at the origin, $y = \frac{1}{4p}x^2$, where $p$ is the distance from the vertex to the focus.  
> **Note:** The word *focus* here is not a mental concentration but a geometric point that helps define the shape.  
Parabolic shapes are everywhere because gravity makes projectiles follow a parabola when air resistance is small. The path of a basketball shot, the arc of water from a garden sprinkler, and the shape of a satellite dish (which reflects signals to its focus) are all parabolic. Designers use the equation to aim dishes so that signals from a distant satellite all meet at the receiver placed at the focus.

An **ellipse** looks like a stretched circle. It is the set of points whose total distance to two fixed points (the foci) is constant. Its equation with centre at the origin is  
$$ \frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1 $$  
where $a$ and $b$ are the semi‑major and semi‑minor axes.  
> **Definition:** The *major axis* is the longest diameter of the ellipse, and the *minor axis* is the shortest.  
Ellipses describe planetary orbits: according to Kepler’s first law, each planet moves around the Sun in an elliptical path with the Sun at one focus. The same idea is used for the design of race tracks, where the straight sections are joined by elliptical curves to allow smooth turning at high speed. In optics, an elliptical mirror can focus light from one focus to the other, useful in telescopes and solar collectors.

A **hyperbola** consists of two separate curves that open away from each other. Its standard equation (center at the origin) is  
$$ \frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1 $$  
Each branch approaches two straight lines called *asymptotes* but never touches them.  
> **Common mistake:** Thinking a hyperbola is a “broken” circle; it is actually formed by the difference of distances to two foci being constant, not the sum.  
Hyperbolas appear in the pattern of a radio‑direction‑finding antenna (the “lobes” of the reception pattern), in the shape of a cooling tower’s cross‑section, and in the paths of objects moving faster than the speed of sound, creating a sonic boom cone whose cross‑section is a hyperbola.

> **Remember:** The same simple definitions—equal distance to a point and a line (parabola), constant sum or difference of distances to two points (ellipse, hyperbola)—produce a wide variety of practical shapes. Recognising these patterns lets engineers, astronomers and designers translate real‑world problems into algebraic equations that can be solved with confidence.

practice.q: Write the standard equation of a circle with centre $(3,-2)$ and radius $5$.
practice.a:
The centre is $(h,k)=(3,-2)$ and $r=5$. Substitute into $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$:
$$ (x-3)^2 + (y+2)^2 = 25. $$

practice.q: A parabola opens upward with vertex at the origin and focus at $(0,2)$. Find its equation.
practice.a:
For a vertical parabola, $4p$ is the coefficient of $x^2$ in $y = \frac{1}{4p}x^2$. The focus is $p$ units from the vertex, so $p=2$. Hence $4p = 8$ and the equation is
$$ y = \frac{1}{8}x^2 \quad\text{or}\quad x^2 = 8y. $$

practice.q: Determine the eccentricity of the ellipse $\displaystyle \frac{x^2}{25} + \frac{y^2}{9}=1$.
practice.a:
Here $a^2=25$, $b^2=9$, so $a=5$, $b=3$. Compute $c$ using $c^2 = a^2 - b^2$:
$$ c^2 = 25 - 9 = 16 \;\Rightarrow\; c = 4. $$
Eccentricity $e = \dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{4}{5}=0.8$.

practice.q: Find the equation of a hyperbola with centre at the origin, transverse axis along the $x$‑axis, vertices at $(\pm6,0)$ and foci at $(\pm10,0)$.
practice.a:
Vertices give $a=6$, so $a^2=36$. Foci give $c=10$, so $c^2=100$. Use $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$ to find $b^2$:
$$ b^2 = c^2 - a^2 = 100 - 36 = 64. $$
Standard form:
$$ \frac{x^2}{36} - \frac{y^2}{64} = 1. $$

practice.q: A satellite dish is shaped like a paraboloid whose cross‑section is the parabola $y = \frac{1}{4}x^2$. If the dish is $12\,$m wide (distance between the two points where $y=3$), find the depth of the dish (the $y$‑coordinate of the vertex to the rim).
practice.a:
The width $12\,$m means the points are at $x = \pm6$. Plug into the equation:
$$ y = \frac{1}{4}(6)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\cdot36 = 9. $$
So the rim is at $y=9$. The vertex is at the origin $(0,0)$. Depth = $9-0 = 9\,$m.

practice.q: An ellipse has one focus at $(0,0)$ and the other at $(8,0)$. The sum of the distances from any point on the ellipse to the two foci is $10$. Write the equation of the ellipse in standard form.
practice.a:
The distance between foci is $2c = 8$, so $c = 4$. The constant sum $2a = 10$, so $a = 5$. Use $c^2 = a^2 - b^2$ to find $b$:
$$ b^2 = a^2 - c^2 = 5^2 - 4^2 = 25 - 16 = 9. $$
The centre is midway between the foci, at $(4,0)$. Translate the standard form $\frac{x'^2}{a^2} + \frac{y'^2}{b^2}=1$ with $x' = x-4$, $y' = y$:
$$ \frac{(x-4)^2}{25} + \frac{y^2}{9} = 1. $$

recap: This lesson explains that conic sections are the curves formed when a plane cuts a double‑napped cone. By changing the angle of the cut we obtain circles, ellipses, parabolas, or hyperbolas, each with a simple geometric definition. The section also introduces eccentricity, a single number that tells us which type of conic we have, and shows real‑world examples of each shape.

key_terms.meaning: A curve produced by intersecting a plane with a double‑napped cone.
Two identical cones joined at their tips, one pointing up and one down.
The ratio c/a that measures how stretched a conic is; e<1 ellipse, e=1 parabola, e>1 hyperbola, e=0 circle.
A fixed point used in the definitions of parabola, ellipse and hyperbola.
A fixed line used together with the focus to define a parabola.
The point on a conic closest to the focus; for a parabola it is the tip, for an ellipse or hyperbola it is one of the ends of the major axis.
The longest diameter of an ellipse or hyperbola, passing through both foci.
The set of all points that satisfy a given geometric condition.

quiz.q: What shape do you get when the cutting plane is perpendicular to the axis of the cone?
quiz.why: A perpendicular cut gives a circular cross‑section.

quiz.q: In the definition of a parabola, what must be equal for any point on the curve?
options: Distance to the focus and to the directrix
Sum of distances to two foci
Difference of distances to two foci
quiz.why: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix.

quiz.q: Which conic has eccentricity exactly equal to 1?
For an ellipse, the sum of the distances from any point on the curve to the two foci is:
options: Constant and greater than the distance between the foci
Constant and equal to the distance between the foci
Constant and less than the distance between the foci
quiz.why: The defining property of an ellipse is a constant sum larger than the focal separation.

quiz.q: If the absolute difference of distances to two fixed points is constant, the curve is a:
quiz.why: A constant difference of distances defines a hyperbola.

quiz.q: Which real‑world object is best modelled by a parabola?
quiz.why: Satellite dishes use the reflective property of a parabola to focus signals.

flashcards.back: A curve formed by intersecting a plane with a double‑napped cone.
e = c / a, the ratio of distance from centre to focus (c) over distance from centre to vertex (a).

flashcards.front: State the geometric definition of a circle.
flashcards.back: All points in a plane at a fixed distance (radius) from a single centre point.

flashcards.front: How is a parabola defined using focus and directrix?
flashcards.back: Every point on the curve is equally distant from a fixed point (focus) and a fixed line (directrix).

flashcards.front: What is the sum of distances property of an ellipse?
flashcards.back: For any point on the ellipse, the sum of its distances to the two foci is constant.
The absolute difference of the distances from any point on the hyperbola to the two foci is constant.

flashcards.front: When does a conic become a circle in terms of eccentricity?
Give a real‑world example of each conic: circle, parabola, ellipse, hyperbola.
flashcards.back: Circle: clock face; Parabola: satellite dish; Ellipse: planetary orbit; Hyperbola: radar tracking curves.
